headline: BoC Holds at 2.25% as GDP Contracts and Tariff Supports Expand
executive_summary:
The Bank of Canada held its policy rate at 2.25% on March 18, keeping the Bank Rate at 2.5% and the deposit rate at 2.20%, amid a quarterly GDP contraction of −0.6% annualized.2

Statistics Canada's advance manufacturing indicator showed total factory sales rose 3.8% in February, led by transportation equipment, even as year-over-year manufacturing GDP remained −2.5%.3 Retail sales climbed 1.1% to $70.7 billion in January, driven by motor vehicle and parts dealers, while the Industrial Product Price Index gained 5.4% year-over-year in February and the Raw Materials Price Index surged 8.6%.6 In Newfoundland and Labrador, the NL Housing Corporation Three-Apartment Home Development advanced to Under Review.6 Alberta's Beacon AI Centers Heartland Project was cancelled.6

Ottawa extended Employment Insurance temporary measures to support workers hit by tariffs, raised the federal minimum wage, and extended financial supports for post-secondary students.789 Minister Mélanie Joly and Norway's Sigrun Aasland signed a joint statement on research cooperation, while Minister David McGuinty highlighted $900 million to boost defence innovation and quantum technology.1011

Interprovincial trade in manufactured goods rose 0.7% to $167.4 billion in 2024, while wholesale interprovincial trade advanced 1.5%, underscoring modest internal demand growth even as Canada's population reached 41,472,081 on January 1, 2026.1213 Foreign investors purchased $46.7 billion of Canadian securities in January—an unprecedented monthly inflow into Canadian bonds—signalling continued external confidence in Canadian sovereign debt despite the GDP contraction.14

national.analysis:
The Bank of Canada's March 18 decision held the overnight rate at 2.25%, the Bank Rate at 2.5%, and the deposit rate at 2.20%, pausing after prior easing as real GDP contracted at a −0.6% annualized pace.8% year-over-year—inside the 1–3% target band—and unemployment at 6.7%.15

Advance manufacturing data for February showed a 3.8% monthly increase in factory sales, the strongest signal from that sector in months, even though manufacturing GDP on a year-over-year basis stood at −2.5%.3 Wholesale trade GDP rose 1.7% month-over-month, while transportation and warehousing gained 0.7%.15 Utilities GDP jumped 2.7% month-over-month, though it remained −0.8% year-over-year.15

Investment in building construction fell $448.3 million (−1.9%) to $23.4 billion in January, even as housing starts held at 250,900 units annualized.16 Urban transit ridership dropped 4.1% year-over-year in January to 126.6 million passenger trips, or 5.4 million fewer rides.17 The business opening rate slipped 0.2 percentage points to 4.8% in December, matching the closure rate.18

The federal government announced it is extending EI temporary measures to cushion tariff-impacted workers and raising the federal minimum wage.78 Private nursing and residential care facility revenue rose 7.1% to $20.6 billion in 2024, partly reflecting an aging population: Canadians aged 65 and older now represent 19.0% of the population.7 billion in Canadian securities in January—led by record bond purchases—while Canadians bought $11.4 billion in foreign securities, maintaining a large net inflow.14 Canadian-resident return trips from the United States fell 22.0% year-over-year in January, and US-resident trips to Canada dipped 0.3%.20

industry_executive_summary:
Management of companies (NAICS 55) posted the sharpest monthly contraction of any tracked sector, falling 2.1% month-over-month and collapsing 19.0% year-over-year as of the latest StatCan Table 36-10-0434-01 release, signalling a profound structural retrenchment in corporate holding activity across Canada.6% in the most recent quarter, with unemployment holding at 6.7% and CPI at 1.8% year-over-year, confirming a fragile macro environment in which sector-level divergences are widening.2

Utilities (NAICS 22) led all sectors with a 2.7% monthly gain, while Wholesale Trade (NAICS 41) advanced 1.7% and Manufacturing (NAICS 31-33) rose 1.2% month-over-month — the latter supported by Statistics Canada's advance estimate showing total manufacturing sales up 3.8% in February 2026, with the largest gains in the transportation equipment subsector.3 Interprovincial trade in manufactured goods edged up 0.7% to $167.4 billion in 2024, while wholesale goods rose 1.5%, underscoring modest but real goods-flow momentum even as headline GDP weakened.4

A notable cross-sector pattern is the simultaneous contraction in Agriculture (-0.8% M/M), Mining & Energy (-0.9% M/M), and Professional Services (-0.1% M/M), while labour-market supports are being reinforced: the federal government raised the federal minimum wage on March 24 and extended Employment Insurance temporary measures for tariff-impacted workers on March 20, reflecting Ottawa's read that goods-producing and service-sector workers face mounting income risk.5

goodsIndustries.name: Agriculture
goodsIndustries.analysis:
• Agriculture (NAICS 11) contracted 0.8% month-over-month in the latest StatCan Table 36-10-0434-01 reading, partially reversing a strong year-over-year gain of 7.6% that remains the highest among all goods-producing sectors tracked.1
  • The 7.6% annual expansion in agricultural GDP reflects sustained output growth over the past year, though the February monthly decline suggests seasonal or supply-side friction entering early 2026.1
  • Wheat prices stood at $591.75 per bushel as of March 24, 2026, while Soybeans were at $1,154.00 and Soybean Meal at $322.40, providing mixed revenue signals for crop and oilseed producers depending on contract timing.2
  • The Raw Materials Price Index rose 8.6% year-over-year in February 2026, a figure that weighs on input costs for agricultural operations reliant on fertilizers and energy-linked inputs.3
  • Interprovincial trade of manufactured goods — which includes agri-food processing — rose just 0.7% to $167.4 billion in 2024, suggesting limited downstream absorption of primary agricultural output growth.4
  • NAICS 111 (Crop production) and NAICS 112 (Animal production) are the dominant subsectors; the monthly dip likely reflects seasonal planting-period lulls rather than structural demand destruction given the robust 7.6% annual figure.1
